subject: English
summaryPoints: Zero conditional sentences express universal truths, scientific facts, and automatic general causes and effects using simple present tense in both clauses.

First conditional sentences express realistic, possible conditions in the present/future and their probable results using the simple present in the if-clause and 'will/can/may + V1' in the main clause.
The order of clauses in conditional sentences is reversible; when the if-clause begins the sentence, a comma is mandatory, but no comma is needed when the main clause comes first.

Prefixes are morphological bound morphemes affixed before base words that change meaning: 'ante-' (before), 'anti-' (opposing/against), 'en-' (cause to be/put into), 'dis-' (negation/removal), and 'un-' (not).
Phrasal verbs based on 'call' convey distinct idioms: 'call for' (demand/require), 'call off' (cancel), 'call up' (recollect/summon), and 'call back' (return a telephone call).
Informative report writing requires an objective account answering who, when, where, and what occurred based on factual evidence.

formulas.label: Zero Conditional Formula (Factual/Universal Truth)
formulas.expr: If + Subject + V1(-s/-es) [Simple Present] + , + Subject + V1(-s/-es) [Simple Present]

formulas.label: First Conditional Formula (Probable Future Result)
formulas.expr: If + Subject + V1(-s/-es) [Simple Present] + , + Subject + will/can/may/shall + V1(base)

formulas.label: Negative First Conditional (Unless Structure)
formulas.expr: Unless + Subject + V1(-s/-es) [Simple Present] + , + Subject + will/can + V1(base)  [Unless = If not]

examTip: Never use future modal auxiliaries ('will', 'shall', 'would') inside the conditional 'if-clause' in First Conditional questions. Incorrect: 'If it will rain tomorrow...'; Correct: 'If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.'

keyDefinitions.definition: A conditional structure used to articulate general truths, scientific facts, or habitual causal relationships where the result is guaranteed.
A conditional structure used to describe realistic, attainable present or future conditions and their probable outcomes.
An affix added to the beginning of a root or base word to modify its semantic meaning.
An organism or animal that is native to and exclusively found in a specific geographic habitat or region (e.g., Walia Ibex, Ethiopian Wolf).
